task.goal: Reduce lost medication instruction sheets in a shared home while keeping them private.
hard_constraints: Two adults, existing folders and no scanning service or new lockbox.
Do not change doses or replace clinician advice; each person controls their own papers.
Test retrieval time and misfiling after one month without exposing diagnoses.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One private home for each person’s sheets
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make a single, predictable storage location the main safeguard against loss. Each adult chooses a neutral symbol for their existing folder and keeps it in a fixed shelf position. Inside, place instruction sheets in closed envelopes, with one instruction set per envelope. The owner assigns each envelope a neutral code and files it in code order. A private paper key inside the folder connects codes to the owner’s descriptions. Labels visible on the shelf contain no medication names or diagnoses.

Each adult handles only their own contents and returns an envelope immediately after reading it. New sheets go directly into that person’s folder; the owner decides how to distinguish current and older instructions without changing the instructions or discarding anything on the other person’s behalf.

This needs existing folders, envelopes, paper labels and enough shelf space. It could work because every sheet has one destination, reducing decisions about where to put it. It assumes both adults accept the return habit. Closed envelopes provide everyday visual privacy, but do not prevent deliberate access; this is unsuitable if privacy requires protection from intentional snooping.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before setup, each owner privately times retrieval of two instruction sets from their current arrangement. After one month, repeat with the same sets, starting from the same location. Each owner also checks whether their sheets are in their assigned envelopes and folder, reporting only elapsed times and a misfiling count. Keep names, contents and the private key out of shared results. No improvement in retrieval, or any increase in misfiling, challenges the benefit of the fixed-home rule.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A private locator index across existing folders
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep papers in the existing folders that each owner finds useful, but introduce a private address system. Each adult gives their folders neutral location codes and their instruction envelopes neutral item codes. A paper locator, kept inside that adult’s own closed envelope on the shelf, maps their personally meaningful descriptions to folder and envelope codes. Exterior labels disclose only codes. Each person alone creates and updates their locator and handles their papers.

The main mechanism is separating finding a document from remembering where it was filed. This can suit someone whose instruction sheets belong with several different groups of paperwork and who would otherwise create duplicate or competing storage places. Whenever the owner moves an instruction envelope, they update its address immediately. New sheets receive an address before filing.

Implementation requires only existing folders, envelopes, paper labels and shelf space. It assumes the owner can maintain and interpret a short index. Its main weakness is an outdated locator: it adds a maintenance step and may be slower than a single folder for a small collection. Envelopes must conceal their contents adequately; coded labels alone do not provide access control.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record private retrieval times for two existing instruction sets before adding the locator. After one month, each owner retrieves those sets using their index and privately checks every indexed address against the actual envelope location. Share only retrieval times and counts of incorrect addresses or misfiled sheets. Compare against the original arrangement: slower retrieval or stale addresses would argue against retaining the index. Do not copy medication descriptions into the shared results.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A visible checkout signal for papers in use
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a circulation rule to address sheets that disappear after someone reads or carries them. Each adult keeps their instruction sets in closed, neutrally coded envelopes in their own existing folder. For each envelope, make a matching paper label that normally rests inside the folder beside it. When the owner removes an envelope, they leave its label protruding from the folder as a checkout signal. The label shows only the neutral code.

Each adult also designates one closed envelope on the shelf as their temporary return pocket. After use, papers go either directly back into their coded envelope or into that owner’s return pocket. At a personally chosen daily routine, the owner checks protruding labels, retrieves outstanding papers and empties their return pocket. Neither adult opens or sorts the other’s papers.

The mechanism makes unfinished returns noticeable and gives loose sheets a defined landing place. It needs envelopes, labels and existing folders, and assumes most losses occur during use rather than initial filing. It will fail if checkout signals are routinely skipped or ignored. Neutral signals conceal medical content but reveal that paperwork is outstanding; both adults must find that acceptable. Closed envelopes offer visual privacy, not security against deliberate opening.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before starting, privately time retrieval of two instruction sets and count sheets outside their intended locations. After one month, repeat and have each owner inspect their own checkout signals and return pocket. Report only times, misfiling counts and unmatched-signal counts. Compare with the original arrangement. Persistent outstanding signals, accumulated return-pocket papers or unchanged retrieval times would suggest that the circulation routine adds work without solving the loss problem.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Move the folder, keep the sheets together
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each adult’s existing folder a portable reading surface: bring the whole folder to wherever instructions are needed, open it flat, and read sheets resting inside it. Individual sheets never travel separately around the home. After reading, the owner closes the papers inside an envelope and the folder, then returns the whole folder to the shelf.

The main mechanism is reducing separation during handling. A whole folder is more noticeable than a loose sheet, and keeping it underneath the papers makes it easier to gather everything before leaving the reading spot. This differs from tracking individual documents: it prevents a common opportunity for separation rather than recording where a removed sheet went.

Each adult chooses a neutral exterior label and controls all organization inside their own folder. Envelopes conceal instruction text when the folder is closed. Neither adult checks, sorts or returns the other’s contents. Keep the original instructions intact; this changes paper handling only, without interpreting instructions or changing doses.

Implementation needs two existing folders, sufficiently large envelopes, paper labels and shelf space. It assumes each collection is small enough to carry comfortably and most use happens at home. It may offer little benefit if losses happen before papers reach the folder, or if individual sheets must frequently accompany appointments. Closed folders and envelopes provide visual privacy, but cannot prevent deliberate opening.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before starting, each owner privately times retrieval of two instruction sheets using their current arrangement and counts missing or incorrectly filed sheets. After one month, repeat retrieval from the same starting point, including opening the envelope and finding the actual sheet. Each owner privately checks their own folder and usual reading locations for separated or misfiled sheets. Share only elapsed times and counts, with no document titles, medication names or diagnoses. Compare with the original arrangement: continued loose-sheet losses or consistently slower retrieval would challenge the approach. This small check can reveal practical failure, but cannot establish long-term reliability.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check papers before leaving their source
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Prevent loss before instruction sheets reach home by making collection and transport a deliberate checkpoint. Each adult takes an empty, opaque envelope to appointments or other places where they expect paper instructions. Before leaving, the owner gathers any sheets actually issued, checks that all pages of each instruction set are present, and puts them directly into the envelope. If a referenced page appears absent, they ask the issuing staff about it; they do not reconstruct medical instructions themselves.

At home, the owner transfers the papers into their existing folder and checks the page count against a small tally written inside the transport envelope. The envelope stays with the papers until that check is complete. Exterior labels contain only a neutral personal symbol. Each adult handles and checks only their own papers; the other adult does not act as an auditor.

The mechanism is checking completeness at the point where missing papers can still be recovered, then preserving the collected batch during transport. This targets losses before filing, which a home storage rule cannot repair. It requires envelopes, paper labels, existing folders and shelf space. It assumes at least some losses occur during collection or travel and that the owner can pause to check the papers. It provides visual privacy, not protection against deliberate opening. Existing instructions remain intact, and clinical advice and doses are unchanged.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before starting, each adult privately times retrieval of two existing instruction sets and counts missing or misfiled sheets. After one month, repeat those retrievals and inspect their own filing. Also check whether any newly received batches arrived with fewer pages than recorded at collection. Share only retrieval times, misfiling counts and batch discrepancies, without titles or medical information. Compare with the previous handling routine. Continued transport discrepancies or increased misfiling challenge the approach. If no new sheets arrive during the month, the main mechanism remains untested; the retrieval check alone cannot establish its benefit.

EXPAND.title: Move the folder, not individual sheets
EXPAND.proposal:
Change the unit carried around the home: each adult carries their entire existing folder whenever they need instructions. The owner puts each instruction set in an opaque envelope inside that folder, using neutral exterior labels. At consultation, they place the folder beneath the papers, open only one set, and put it back before closing or moving the folder. They return the closed folder to its shelf position after use. Neither adult handles the other’s contents.

The mechanism reduces opportunities to leave individual sheets at reading locations or separate pages during transport. Unlike the prior fixed-home approach, success depends on keeping papers with a larger object throughout use, rather than remembering to return a separately carried envelope afterward. New sheets join the owner’s folder before their first home consultation. If something is missing, the owner checks their last consultation location privately.

This requires only folders, envelopes, labels and shelf space. It assumes the folder is manageable to carry and consultations usually happen somewhere it can lie open. It may become burdensome with a large collection or expose unrelated contents when opened near someone else; owners should consult it privately. Closed envelopes conceal contents from casual view but cannot prevent intentional access. The routine changes paper handling only, never doses or clinical instructions.
EXPAND.experiment: Each adult owns a one-month trial and records only retrieval seconds, missing or misfiled sets, and instances when carrying the folder was inconvenient. Before starting, privately time retrieval of two sets under the simple fixed-folder arrangement. After one month, repeat those retrievals and inspect their own contents for misfiling; share only numbers. Stop earlier if carrying the folder causes a spill or unwanted visibility. Retain the rule only if fewer misplaced papers or faster retrieval justify the carrying burden; equal performance with more inconvenience favors the simpler fixed-home rule.

EXPAND.title: An owner-only recovery sweep
EXPAND.proposal:
Add a recovery process for sheets that escape normal filing. Each adult chooses a weekly household routine during which they privately inspect the places where they personally read or unload papers. They collect only their own recognizable instruction sheets into a closed envelope, then return them to their own existing folder on the shelf. The folder and envelope use neutral labels.

If an adult encounters an ambiguous paper, they leave it unexamined and tell the other adult only its location. Its owner decides whether to collect and file it. No one reads, sorts or discards another person’s papers. Newly received sheets still go directly into the owner’s folder, and ordinary consultation ends with returning them there.

The new mechanism is periodic recovery from actual locations, independent of remembering to make a checkout signal. It could catch omissions that the prior checkout approach misses when someone forgets both the signal and the return. It also adds searching work and allows papers to remain misplaced until the next sweep; it is unsuitable if unattended papers would create unacceptable exposure.

Implementation needs existing folders, envelopes, paper labels and a few minutes of owner time each week. It assumes each person knows their usual paper-use locations and can inspect them without searching the other person’s belongings. Missing instructions that remain unfound require the owner to seek another copy from the issuing clinician or pharmacy; nobody reconstructs advice from memory.
EXPAND.experiment: Each adult runs the routine for one month, privately recording sweep minutes and the number of misplaced sheets recovered. Time retrieval of two instruction sets before setup and again after one month; privately count remaining misfilings. Share only times and counts. Compare with the prior fixed-folder rule: recovery must reduce missing papers or retrieval time enough to justify the weekly search. Stop if sweeps repeatedly encounter the other adult’s private material, or if papers remain exposed between sweeps. Finding nothing while adding work is evidence to drop the routine.

EXPAND.title: Reconcile papers at the point of receipt
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a brief owner-controlled completeness check before incoming instructions join household paperwork. When either adult receives a new instruction set, that owner checks the pages while they are still together, asks the issuer about any apparent missing pages, and puts the complete set directly into an envelope. On the envelope’s inside flap, the owner records its page count and a personally meaningful identifier; the outside carries only a neutral label. At home, the owner checks the count once more before placing the envelope in their existing folder on the shelf.

The mechanism catches loss during the transition from receiving papers to storing them. The prior fixed-home route starts with a destination but cannot establish whether all pages ever reached it. This route establishes a private completeness reference before transport. On later retrieval, a count mismatch prompts the owner to inspect their own transport belongings and usual unloading location, then contact the issuer if necessary. A matching count is only a basic check: it does not prove that the pages are correct or clinically current.

This needs envelopes available when papers are received, existing folders and paper labels. It assumes the owner receives the papers personally and can briefly check them. No second adult verifies contents. Owners retain control over older papers and ask the issuing professional about uncertain instructions; the count never determines medication use. Opaque envelopes provide casual visual privacy, not protection against deliberate opening.
EXPAND.experiment: Each adult owns a one-month trial covering naturally received instructions; do not generate extra medical visits. Record only reconciliation time and discrepancies caught. Before starting and after one month, privately time retrieval of two existing sets and count misfilings, sharing only numeric results. Compare with placing incoming sheets directly into a private folder: count checking must catch otherwise missed loss without worsening retrieval or creating excessive work. Stop if carrying envelopes or checking counts proves impractical. If no new papers arrive, the trial cannot establish the entry-check benefit; a private rehearsal with ordinary nonmedical pages can assess usability only.

EXPAND.title: Improvement to the fixed-home mechanism: contain interrupted filing
EXPAND.proposal:
Keep the strongest simple route: each adult controls one existing folder in a fixed shelf position, with instruction sets in closed envelopes bearing neutral codes and a private key inside. Add one owner-specific closed envelope marked with a neutral symbol for papers whose filing was interrupted. This repairs a gap between knowing the destination and completing the return.

Each owner puts new or consulted sheets directly into their assigned envelope. If interrupted, they put the whole set into their temporary envelope before leaving it. At the next folder opening, the owner files its contents before taking out another set, unless instructions are needed immediately; then they finish after that consultation. Nobody sorts the other adult’s papers. This borrows the return pocket from the circulation route without requiring checkout tokens or a daily sweep.

The additional resource is one envelope per adult. It assumes interruptions allow a brief containment action. Owners check that closed envelopes conceal print; nesting available envelopes can help if needed. This provides casual visual privacy, not protection against intentional opening. If that protection is necessary, the available resources cannot meet it.

The pocket can become a second permanent filing location. If it repeatedly accumulates papers, the owner drops it and carries their whole folder during consultation, returning each set before closing the folder. Missing papers prompt a private check of the pocket and last use location, followed by a request to the issuer for replacement if necessary. Filing choices never determine doses or replace clinician advice.
EXPAND.experiment: Each adult privately times retrieval of two sets and counts misfiled or missing sets before setup and after one month. Compare with their current feasible fixed-folder practice. During the month, record only interrupted returns contained, pocket backlogs encountered, and approximate extra handling time. Share numbers only. Stop using the pocket if it causes a failed retrieval, unwanted visibility, or repeated backlog; use the whole-folder fallback. Faster retrieval or fewer misfilings must justify the added handling. No interruptions means the trial provides little evidence for this addition.

EXPAND.title: Owner acceptance at shared-paper handoffs
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent instruction sheets from disappearing when one adult moves household papers for the other. The mechanism is explicit transfer of custody at an already occurring moment: clearing a shared surface or passing over incoming papers. It is most useful when shared handling, rather than the owner’s own filing, causes losses.

Each adult chooses a neutral symbol for an existing folder and a closed receiving envelope on the shelf. Agree that a receiving envelope is an accepted delivery location. An adult may deposit papers there only when ownership is already known without reading medical contents, such as a closed envelope addressed to the other person. They give a brief private location notice during their ordinary contact. The receiving owner checks the envelope when receiving that notice, then files their own sets in closed envelopes inside their folder. Exterior labels contain no medication names or diagnoses.

Loose or ambiguous papers are not guessed into either person’s folder. The finder avoids examining them and privately tells the other adult their location. Until the owner collects them or accepts a specific location, the finder retains responsibility for communicating where they remain. If contact is interrupted, known-owner papers go into the agreed receiving envelope; ambiguous papers remain together at their existing location. If that location is exposed or the instructions are needed immediately, make direct contact rather than treating an unread notice as acceptance.

This needs envelopes, labels, shelf space and both adults’ agreement. It cannot solve the owner losing papers after filing. If handoffs rarely occur, direct owner filing is simpler. Each owner alone resolves missing sets, contacting the issuer for replacements when necessary; neither interprets or changes the other’s instructions.
EXPAND.experiment: For one month, each adult privately records the number of actual shared-paper handoffs, failed transfers, and extra handling minutes. Before setup and after one month, time retrieval of two instruction sets and count misfilings or missing sets. Share only times and counts. Compare with ordinary direct owner filing, without deliberately exposing medical papers. Stop routing through receiving envelopes if they accumulate unnoticed papers or cause a failed retrieval; use direct personal handover instead. Any privacy incident also stops the trial. If there are no relevant handoffs, the proposed benefit remains untested.
